\section{Finite Ramsey barrier: problem and proof architecture}

Write \(R(3,k)\) for the least \(n\) such that every graph on \(n\) vertices
contains either a triangle or an independent set of order \(k\).  The current
dynamic survey records
\[
  100\le R(3,18)\le 120;
\]
see Radziszowski's continuously maintained table~\cite{Radziszowski2026}.
The public construction of Nagda, Raghavan, and Thakurta supplies a
triangle-free graph on \(99\) vertices with independence number \(17\),
thereby certifying the lower endpoint~\cite{NagdaRaghavanThakurta2026}.
Extending that graph by one vertex produces a natural, but logically delicate,
local search around the next possible certificate.

This part studies one labelled \(100\)-vertex extension \(H\).  The graph
has no independent \(18\)-set but has a unique triangle.  It is therefore a
near miss, not a Ramsey graph.  We ask a deliberately local question: how
many \emph{original} edges must be deleted before the triangle can be removed
while arbitrary original nonedges are allowed to change into edges?  This
asymmetric edit model makes additions completely free; consequently, a lower
bound in this model is stronger than a lower bound obtained by fixing the
nonedges or by restricting the total symmetric-difference distance.

The principal result is a proof-carrying lower bound of seven on that local
deletion radius.  The argument has four independently inspectable layers.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item A direct graph check establishes the seed identity, its unique
  triangle, and the absence of an independent \(18\)-set.
\item The unique triangle gives an exhaustive three-way branch split.  A
  previous proof-carrying package excludes total deletion budget at most
  five, reducing the new layer to exact budget six.
\item Each exact-six branch is translated into a finite CNF \emph{relaxation}
  of the graph problem.  All structural clauses are reconstructed from the
  seed; the independent-set clauses are validated as universally sound.
\item CaDiCaL emits a DRAT refutation for each branch, and a separately pinned
  \texttt{drat-trim} executable verifies every refutation.  Solver status
  strings are not used as proof evidence.
\end{enumerate}

This layering is important.  An unsatisfiable CNF proves the graph claim only
after formula soundness and branch completeness have been established.  A
solver's report of unsatisfiability proves the CNF claim only after an
independently checkable proof trace has been accepted.  We record both
implications explicitly.

The computation is also informative about what remains open.  We first tested
the next deletion layer, exact budget seven, with one bounded solver call in
each branch.  Every call reached its wall-time limit before producing a
separated model or a proof.  A follow-up branch-1 analysis proves the necessary
degree cap \(\deg(v)\le17\) and thereby excludes \(87.5813\ldots\%\) of its raw
six-edge residual deletion sets.  A deletion-first pilot encoded that lift and
initially encountered two apparent exact independent-set separator stalls.
An order-aware reconstruction showed that both stalls were vertex-order
artefacts: reverse ordering returned the requested witness batches in
milliseconds.  Seven repaired gates then spent their bounded walls in the
master after fast separation, but again produced neither a verified model nor
a checked global proof.  A subsequent proof-carrying generalized-core route
produced four stronger, checked singleton no-goods for branch~1: every
satisfying assignment of the common relaxation must preserve each of four
named seed edges.  Their CNFs were rebuilt byte for byte without the
production encoder and their DRAT traces were replayed by separately built
checker binaries on two architectures.  A checked satisfying model shows that
the common relaxation is nonempty, although that model itself contains an
independent \(18\)-set.  The singleton clauses exclude an additional
\(1307748575589\) residual supports beyond the degree cap, about
\(2.431110\%\) of its survivors.  This is a rigorous family-level pruning
result, but it leaves branch~1 and the overall exact-seven problem open.  A
subsequent exact projection found \(396\) forced original-nonedge assignments
but no additional pure deletion-support clause.  We then proved, using the
checked budget-six obstruction, that every feasible branch-1 repair has a
maximal-triangle-free representative.  Combining a full all-pair encoding of
that normal form with the complete \(530525\)-mask union gives a fixed CNF with
\(639290\) variables and \(1972360\) clauses.  Independent reconstruction was
byte-exact, but its single \(300\)-second bounded call timed out with no model
or proof.  We record this and every other unresolved endpoint as
\textsc{unknown}; none is evidence either for or against the existence of a
seven-deletion repair.

\paragraph{Claim boundary.}
The theorem concerns one fixed, labelled seed and one one-sided edit metric.
It neither constructs a \(100\)-vertex \((3,18)\)-Ramsey graph nor rules out
such graphs elsewhere in the search space.  Thus it does not improve either
endpoint of the globally tabulated interval for \(R(3,18)\).  The value of the
result is instead methodological and local: it gives a complete,
proof-carrying obstruction around a particularly close seed, with all
negative conclusions separated from incomplete search.
